name: Chinese remainder theorem
formula: m_1, \ldots, m_k \text{ pairwise coprime} \implies x \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i} \text{ has one solution modulo } m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k
whenToUse: A number leaves given remainders on division by several coprime numbers. Also to split a hard modulus like $100$ into $4$ and $25$.
example: Find $n$ with $n \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, $n \equiv 3 \pmod 5$, $n \equiv 2 \pmod 7$. The first and last say $n \equiv 2 \pmod{21}$: try $2, 23, 44, \ldots$; $23 \equiv 3 \pmod 5$. So $n \equiv 23 \pmod{105}$.
pitfall: The moduli must be pairwise coprime for a single solution. With moduli $4$ and $6$, conditions can clash or leave a solution only modulo $12$, not $24$.
